lesson_title: Same Lego, New Models: How to Write a Chemical Reaction
hook_text: When magnesium burns, not a single atom disappears. They just swap partners.
clip_script: Light a strip of magnesium and it flares brilliant white and leaves a white powder. Something new has been made. That is a chemical reaction. Think of atoms as Lego blocks. The reactants are the models you start with, magnesium metal and oxygen from the air. The reaction pulls them apart and rebuilds the same blocks into a new model, magnesium oxide. No new blocks, none thrown away. Chemists write it three ways. As a model: grey balls and red balls regrouped. As a word equation: magnesium plus oxygen, arrow, magnesium oxide. The plus means and, the arrow means makes, and it only points one way. And as a chemical equation: 2Mg plus O2 gives 2MgO. Now count the blocks. Left: two magnesium, two oxygen. Right: two magnesium oxide, so two magnesium, two oxygen. Same blocks, new models. That is the whole of chemistry in one line.
visual_style: Slow-motion magnesium flare; grey and red Lego-style balls pull apart and snap into new pairs; the three representations stack on screen and atoms are counted with ticks on each side.
pacing: A flash for the hook, a calm Lego beat, three quick representations, a rhythmic count at the end.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and write methane burning in words and in symbols.
